touristAppeal.label: Worth a Visit

townGuide.characterTag: Granite quarry village and landscape art
townGuide.headline: A distinctive granite story told through art, paths and built heritage
townGuide.intro: Kemnay earns 72 within its own visitor boundary. Place of Origin and the Kemnay Steens turn quarry history into a genuine public-art experience, while a council treasure trail, nine-route map, seasonal Kemnay House opening and the unusual 1831 morthouse support a coherent half-day visit.

suggestedFirstVisit.title: Start with Place of Origin
suggestedFirstVisit.summary: Use the quarry-edge artwork as the anchor, follow the Steens circuit towards the centre, pause at Café 83, then add the churchyard morthouse or a pre-checked Kemnay House event.

dontMiss: Place of Origin and Kemnay Steens Circuit
townGuide.suggestedTime: 3–4 hours; longer on a Kemnay House open day
townGuide.visitorMood: A worthwhile small-town visit built around granite, public art and active exploration rather than a dense conventional attraction list.

features.name: Place of Origin
features.shortDescription: A quarry-edge landscape artwork and viewpoint by John Maine, Brad Goldberg and Glen Onwin, interpreting Kemnay granite and the wider landscape.
features.fullDescription: Paths, carved stone and framed views turn the former quarry edge into Kemnay’s most distinctive public visitor experience. The work began in 1996 and was completed and opened in 2006.

attractionGuide.headline: See Kemnay granite return to its landscape
attractionGuide.intro: Follow the quarry-edge work slowly: carved stone, changing levels and framed views explain why Kemnay granite travelled around the world.
attractionGuide.parking: Use Aquithie Road Car Park and approach through the village route network; do not obstruct quarry access.
attractionGuide.toilets: The former public toilet at Victoria Terrace is closed. Check the current council listing before relying on a facility.
attractionGuide.picnic: No verified formal picnic-table count is published at the artwork.
attractionGuide.foodNote: Café 83 is the strongest current coffee-and-cake stop in the centre.

editorialReview.scoreRationale: Kemnay’s strongest and most distinctive visitor experience, with a coherent quarry story, public access and documented artistic authorship, reduced for exposed weather and path gradients.

features.name: Kemnay House Open Days
features.documentedDateText: Mid-17th-century core; circa 1690 and later 17th-/early-18th-century wings; remodelled 1808 and in the 1830s
features.shortDescription: A Category A laird’s house offering limited seasonal tours, art events and tea in the parlour.
features.fullDescription: The house has a mid-17th-century core and layered additions. Its published 2026 offer is limited to April open days, September North East Open Studios and a December pop-up, so dates must be checked before travel.

attractionGuide.headline: Book a rare look inside Kemnay’s layered laird’s house
attractionGuide.intro: Treat this as an event-led visit, not a daily attraction. Confirm the advertised date, tour time and access arrangements before setting out.
attractionGuide.parking: Parking is on the main drive, with some disabled spaces at the front.
attractionGuide.toilets: Visitor toilet detail is not published; ask when booking if this is essential.
attractionGuide.picnic: The garden is not published as a picnic site.
attractionGuide.foodNote: Tea and home baking are offered on some open days; check the current event.

editorialReview.scoreRationale: A nationally important, richly layered house with genuine guided access and refreshments, reduced sharply because opening is event-led rather than dependable year-round.

features.name: Kemnay Parish Church and Morthouse
features.documentedDateText: Morthouse built 1831; church built 1844–45, enlarged 1871 and remodelled 1928
features.shortDescription: A modest churchyard stop combining an 1831 earth-covered, lead-lined morthouse with the 1844–45 parish church.
features.fullDescription: The bunker-like morthouse is the unusual feature: it was built in 1831 to secure coffins. The present church followed in 1844–45 and was altered in later phases.

editorialReview.scoreRationale: The unusual, precisely dated morthouse gives this churchyard more visitor interest than the church alone, though the experience is chiefly an exterior stop and interior access is not assured.

features.name: Old Laundry, Kemnay House
features.fullDescription: Later to late 18th century, converted to dwelling 1976 and extended 1983. 2-storey, 5-bay, rectangular-plan former washing and brewhouse. Coursed, squared granite with cherry caulking; harled to rear and to extension. SE (PRINCIPAL) ELEVATION: symmetrical with original small openings. Ground floor with window to centre, boarded timber doors in flanking bays and further windows to outer bays; regular fenestration to 1st floor. Slightly set-back single storey extension to outer right. SW ELEVATION: gabled elevation with large window to 1st floor. NW (REAR) ELEVATION: 2 widely-spaced bays to left of centre with windows to each floor, and further window to right at 1st floor. (All openings small). 3 small modern rooflights. Extension set-back at outer left. NE ELEVATION: single storey extension projecting from gabled elevation. 9-pane glazing pattern in timber casement windows to N and S; 12- pane glazing pattern in timber sash and case window to W. Grey slates. Coped ashlar gablehead stacks. Ashlar-coped skews with block skewputts.

features.name: Home Farm, Kemnay House
alternativeNames: KEMNAY HOUSE POLICIES, KEMNAY HOME FARM, LINHAY AND THE STABLES
features.shortDescription: KEMNAY HOUSE POLICIES, KEMNAY HOME FARM, LINHAY AND THE STABLES
features.fullDescription: Probably mid 18th century, altered. Single and 2-storey ranges forming irregular steading with former coachhouse and coachman's house. Squared rubble; some chamfered arrises. SE RANGE (LINHAY AND THE STABLES): slated, piended former coachhouse and coachman's house, converted to 2 dwellings, 1990. All doors boarded timber and mostly small pane glazing patterns in timber sash and case windows. SE (PRINCIPAL) ELEVATION: canopied door to centre bay at ground, windows in flanking bays, voussoired cart arch with door to outer left, and 2-leaf door to right also with flanking windows. 4 windows to 1st floor and 5 rooflights above. NW (REAR) ELEVATION: openings grouped to left. Ground floor with 4 windows flanking stone forestair leading to 1st floor door, this and 2 windows to left all breaking eaves into piended dormerheads, further window to right. Variety of small rooflights. SW ELEVATION: window to centre at ground, and further window breaking eaves into dormerhead above. SW RANGE: piend-roofed range with modern diamond-pattern felt roof covering, boarded timber doors and fixed 6-pane glazing pattern. NE ELEVATION: bay to left of centre with door below louvered opening, further 1st floor opening to right with small ground floor opening and ventilation slit beyond, fixed window to outer right. NW (ENTRANCE) ELEVATION: 2-leaf door to left and further door to right. N RANGE: large, gabled, L-plan range with modern corrugated roof, some openings blocked. Ashlar-coped skews and block skewputts. SE ELEVATION: gabled elevation with voussoired cart arch. NE ELEVATION: 3 doors grouped to right of centre, and projecting bay to outer right. SW ELEVATION: openings blocked and gable to outer left altered.
